text: There: yes. Back: no, and that's what the hash is for. THERE: puppetPost already hands appFaceApp {host, method, path, body}, and appServerPost carries the host inside the packet to your node, where only the forwarder matches it against grants.json to find join's process. The VPS never matches anything. BACK: the reply carries re = the request's hash, and appFaceApp's waiting table maps that hash to the browser request still open on the VPS, which already knows its own host. The host needn't travel back, and better that it doesn't: the hash is the one link between a request and its answer (transport R12), and a second link could disagree with it.

Yes, that hangs together. As a ruling: (1) THE FACE DOMAIN is a setting on your node, default 'app.spirit.<relay domain>' (so 'app.spirit.andyflinn.com'), changeable. Your node uses it for one thing: to turn a request's host into a grant name, 'join.app.spirit.andyflinn.com' minus the face domain = 'join', then look 'join' up in grants.json. (2) DNS, by hand, once: app.spirit.andyflinn.com and *.app.spirit.andyflinn.com both point at the VPS (the wildcard as a CNAME to app.spirit, as you say). (3) Caddy, once: one block for both, with the wildcard certificate by DNS challenge. (4) Every app and every user gets its name by the grant exchange, join exactly like Alice; nothing is special-cased. One thing to decide later, not now: what answers the bare app.spirit.andyflinn.com itself, since no grant has an empty name. I'd say a named refusal until you give it a page. This supersedes §10's flat '*.spirit.<domain>' by one level. Go! = I record it as your ruling in PUPPETS.md §10 and G17, and G17's next slice is the face-domain setting plus the host-to-name step, each declared before it's built.

Agreed. It goes in as superseding §10, quoting both. On members: his words are 'make all other apps and users negotiate their spot in the wildcard space', so users move under *.app.spirit too, and nothing stays at *.spirit. My ask to him says every app and user gets its name by the grant exchange there. I'll write that explicitly and let his answer confirm it. Waiting on his go.

Yes, 'face' is better, and for the reason you give: the label then names appFaceApp's job, the public face of every app and user. The vocabulary already runs that way: face.json switches the listener on, api.face is how an app claims it, the face door. So the default face domain becomes face.spirit.<relay domain>: join.face.spirit.andyflinn.com, alice.face.spirit.andyflinn.com, and one wildcard *.face.spirit.andyflinn.com, still changeable on your node. Go! = I record the whole shape as your ruling: the 'face' default, members and apps both under it, superseding §10's flat *.spirit, quoting both. Then G17's next slice is declared.

Right, I said that badly: two different claims got blurred. An APP claims its segment ('join', 'alice') only through the grant exchange, a faceless packet to appFaceApp, as built. It never touches the face. api.face is something else: the hook by which appFaceApp itself, on the VPS puppet node, takes the listener's visitor traffic, and no other app may take it. So 'face' names appFaceApp's job, and apps only ever get a name in it. I'll write it that way.

Agreed, and it isn't there. 'api.face' is not a host name, just a function in the code (nodeApps hands it to appFaceApp on the VPS). The DNS namespace holds only face.spirit.andyflinn.com and *.face.spirit.andyflinn.com, and the names under it come from grants.

Yes. The grant exchange is two packets, node to node through the relay, even when both ends sit on the same node, as you ruled: 'the negotiation should be a packet even when both ends are on the same node'.

Agreed on what happens, with one correction to the name, from the tree. The negotiation is plain SpiritOS: join, or joe, sends a 'grant' packet through a relay, and nothing on the VPS takes part. But the thing on YOUR node that answers that packet and writes grants.json is, today, appFaceApp too. It's the faceless half, mounted on your node (appFaceApp.js:79 DATASET = 'grants.json', :145 answers verb 'grant'), per your own 'the list is reserved by the appShellApp mapping dataset on the owners personal node'. So appFaceApp runs in two places: on your node, faceless, keeping the table; on the VPS, taking visitor traffic (api.face). My '(nodeApps hands it to appFaceApp on the VPS)' was about the second only. If one name for two jobs is what tripped this, that's worth deciding: keep both halves as appFaceApp, or give the table-keeper its own name.

None. There's no second step. The negotiation you describe, signed packets settling the slot, is exactly what the code calls the 'grant': join or joe asks for a name, your node answers yes or 'name already granted', and the yes is written as one row in grants.json as the record of that exchange. 'Grant' is just the word the code uses for the negotiation's outcome, not an extra permission on top of it. Later, when a visitor asks for join.face.spirit..., your node only looks that row up. It decides nothing new.

Yes, and that sentence simplifies the whole path, if I read it right. The row says who owns the slot, by key: { joe: { to: <joe's key> } }, { join: { to: <join's key> } }. So 'routed to the node owning that slot' is just: look up the host's row and post the request to that key, through the relay, like any packet. It's the same for joe's own node and for join's app-server process, which has a key of its own and is reachable through the relay too. Nothing special for join, and no mapping from a key to a local port on your box. Whether the grantee answers well is, as you say, its own question. This changes wsl-claude's round-trip map, step 5: 'hand to the local app process' becomes 'post to the slot owner's key'. The loopback shortcut (and G18's pipe) becomes an optimisation for later, not the path. Is that what you mean? Go! = yes, and wsl-claude and I rewrite step 5 and G17 that way.
